Pregnancy

Pennyroyal with yogurt in pregnancy: benefits, risks and exposure advice

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A traditional yogurt-and-herb mixture raises two different questions: whether the dairy food is suitable and whether the herb is safe. Pasteurized yogurt can be part of pregnancy nutrition. Pennyroyal needs separate caution; yogurt does not make a potentially toxic herbal product harmless.

Which plant does pennyroyal mean?

The plant named here is Mentha pulegium, an accepted species in the mint family. Common names such as puneh or pennyroyal do not reliably identify every fresh herb, dried mixture or commercial product. American pennyroyal, Hedeoma pulegioides, is another plant also associated with toxic oil. Neither is interchangeable with peppermint or every culinary mint.

Smell, leaf shape and a photograph cannot establish the contents or concentration of a purchased product. Ask about the botanical name, ingredients and preparation. An aromatic plant's essential oils, flavonoids or laboratory activity do not by themselves demonstrate a useful or safe pregnancy treatment.

Yogurt and calcium do not require a herbal corrector

Choose yogurt made from pasteurized milk and follow its storage instructions. Dairy can contribute calcium and protein. Pregnancy does not multiply the recommended calcium intake several-fold: US reference intakes are 1,000 mg a day for ages 19–50 and 1,300 mg for ages 14–18, the same as for nonpregnant people in those age groups. These are total intakes from food and supplements, not instructions to take that amount as a tablet.

There is no established pregnancy evidence that pennyroyal corrects a harmful 'cold nature' of dairy or multiplies calcium absorption. Adequate vitamin D and overall nutrition matter; an added herb is not required. If dairy is unsuitable because of allergy or intolerance, discuss appropriate calcium sources or fortified alternatives with your care team rather than using a herb to compensate.

Traditional treatment claims are not proven benefits

Pennyroyal has been promoted for colds, flu, cough, throat and other respiratory complaints; gas, indigestion, stomach pain or spasms, reflux, nausea, diarrhoea, hiccups and poor appetite; and bad breath. These traditional uses do not establish effectiveness or pregnancy safety. Persistent symptoms deserve assessment, and the herb should not replace treatment for an infection or other illness.

Claims also include helping the gallbladder or liver, acting as an antibiotic, easing headache or fever, lowering blood pressure or blood urea, treating gout, relaxing muscles, calming stress, preventing seizures and bringing on a period. Reliable clinical benefit in pregnancy has not been established for these claims. In particular, serious liver injury and seizures are reported poisoning effects, not reasons to use pennyroyal as a remedy.

Leaves, tea and concentrated oil have different risks

A spoonful of dried herb, an infusion, an extract and an essential oil are different exposures. Oil concentrates constituents including pulegone, which the body can convert to substances that injure organs. Human reports document severe liver and kidney damage, bleeding or clotting problems, neurological injury, breathing or lung complications and death after poisoning. Infant poisoning after herbal tea also shows why 'tea' does not automatically mean harmless.

These reports cannot calculate the risk from one small amount of leaf in a pregnant person's meal. Equally, they do not establish a safe serving, frequency, trimester or yogurt mixture. Avoid intentionally using pennyroyal as a pregnancy remedy, tea, oil or extract; do not rely on 'only occasionally' or 'natural' as a safety rule. Never swallow pennyroyal essential oil. Yogurt does not dilute an unknown product into a proven safe dose or act as an antidote.

Pregnancy loss and other symptoms need careful interpretation

Historical use to stimulate menstruation or end pregnancy is not a safe or dependable method. Severe maternal poisoning can be fatal. There is no basis for saying that only a very large amount can matter, or for recommending an amount to cause contractions. If you need pregnancy-options care, seek a qualified reproductive-health service rather than a herbal method.

Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, dizziness, weakness, confusion, hallucinations, seizures or loss of consciousness can occur in poisoning; a racing heart or throat discomfort also needs assessment after a concerning exposure. Symptoms do not identify the herb or prove a miscarriage. A long list of reported adverse effects is not evidence that every incidental food exposure causes them, and an exposure alone does not establish fetal injury or blame.

What to do after an exposure

If pennyroyal oil may have been swallowed, obtain immediate poison-service or emergency medical advice even if you feel well. Harm can be delayed. For an uncertain leaf or food mixture, stop further use and promptly ask your maternity clinician, pharmacist or poison service for an individual assessment, especially if the species, amount or ingredients are unclear. Do not assume either guaranteed harm or guaranteed safety.

Keep the container or a photograph of its label and note the amount, time, preparation, pregnancy stage, symptoms and other medicines. Follow professional instructions. Do not induce vomiting or use yogurt, food, drink or another herb as a home antidote for suspected poisoning. Do not give a suspected poisoned person food or drink while awaiting advice. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; arrange a driver or ambulance. Do not stop prescribed medicines without advice.

Choose nutrition and symptom care separately

Plain pasteurized yogurt does not need pennyroyal to be a useful food. Choose foods you tolerate and discuss low calcium intake or supplement needs individually. A label saying mint is not enough to confirm the species; do not replace an unidentified product with another unverified herbal blend.

For repeated digestive symptoms, fever, cough, headache or distress, ask your clinician or pharmacist about the cause and pregnancy-appropriate care. Tell them about herbal products as well as prescribed medicines because ingredients and interactions can vary. Food enjoyment, nutrition and treatment are separate decisions; neither traditional use nor a pleasant taste proves medicinal benefit.

When to seek urgent help

Contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy or reduced, stopped or changed usual baby movements. New pelvic pain with possible pregnancy also needs urgent assessment, even without a positive test. Do not wait for an app entry, the next appointment or symptoms to persist.

Get emergency care immediately for heavy vaginal bleeding during pregnancy on its own; severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, or abdominal or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch; or pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding. Breathing difficulty, swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, seizures or loss of consciousness after an exposure also need immediate emergency help. Follow a prescribed allergy emergency plan if applicable. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive or call an ambulance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Check the exact product and preparation with your maternity clinician or pharmacist before use; choose plain pasteurized yogurt rather than adding an unassessed pennyroyal remedy.

After possible oil ingestion, seek immediate poison-service advice even without symptoms. Keep the label and exposure details; do not try a food antidote or induce vomiting.

Discuss calcium intake and persistent symptoms separately. Obtain urgent maternity or emergency assessment for warning signs instead of waiting for tracking or the next visit.

How BeMama can help

BeMama notes can help you bring the food or product name, label ingredients, preparation, amount, time, symptoms and appointment questions to your care team. They cannot identify a plant, certify pregnancy safety, diagnose calcium deficiency or poisoning, or determine fetal wellbeing. Recording must not delay professional advice or urgent care.

When to seek help

Possible swallowed pennyroyal oil needs immediate professional advice even if you feel well. Heavy vaginal bleeding during pregnancy alone, severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, abdominal or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding need emergency care. Breathing difficulty, airway swelling, seizures or loss of consciousness after exposure are emergencies too. Do not drive yourself; arrange a driver or ambulance. Any pregnancy bleeding and reduced or changed usual baby movements need immediate maternity contact. Do not induce vomiting or use food or drink as an antidote.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Plain pasteurized yogurt can provide calcium without an added herb.
  • Mentha pulegium is not interchangeable with every plant called mint or puneh.
  • No safe pregnancy amount or proven benefit of a pennyroyal-yogurt mixture has been established.
  • Possible swallowed pennyroyal oil needs immediate professional advice, even before symptoms.
  • An incidental meal is not proof of fetal harm; record the exact exposure and obtain individual advice without delaying urgent care.

Frequently asked questions

Does pennyroyal have proven traditional benefits in pregnancy?

Traditional claims cover respiratory, digestive and many other conditions, but they do not establish clinical benefit or pregnancy safety. Do not use pennyroyal instead of assessment or prescribed treatment.

Does adding it to yogurt improve calcium absorption?

This benefit has not been established. Pasteurized yogurt can provide calcium on its own; no herbal 'corrector' is required. Individual dietary or supplement advice depends on your age and intake.

Can I eat a little in yogurt occasionally?

A validated safe pregnancy serving or frequency has not been established. Avoid deliberately adding pennyroyal as a remedy. If you already ate a small food mixture, seek advice about the actual plant and preparation rather than assuming harm or dismissing the exposure.

Can pennyroyal cause miscarriage?

It has a history of use to bring on bleeding, but it is an unsafe and unreliable way to end pregnancy and can cause fatal poisoning. No dose is recommended. Exposure does not mean that miscarriage or fetal injury has certainly occurred.

Is tea safer than essential oil?

Concentrated oil has well-documented severe toxicity and must not be swallowed. Tea is a different exposure but is not established as safe in pregnancy; serious poisoning from herbal tea has also been reported in infants. Do not transfer a general culinary-herb rule to pennyroyal.

What if I swallowed oil but feel normal?

Seek immediate poison-service or emergency medical advice. Do not wait for symptoms, induce vomiting or take food or drink as an antidote. Keep the packaging and arrange help; do not drive yourself.

How can BeMama help with a food or herbal exposure?

Use notes to record the product name, ingredients, preparation, amount, time, symptoms and questions for your clinician. Tracking cannot identify the plant, establish fetal safety, diagnose poisoning or replace medical assessment, and must never delay help.

Which symptoms need immediate care?

Heavy pregnancy bleeding alone, severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, abdominal or pelvic pain that hurts with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding require emergency care. Breathing difficulty, airway swelling, seizures or loss of consciousness after an exposure are also emergencies. Do not drive yourself. Any lighter pregnancy bleeding or reduced or changed usual baby movements needs immediate maternity contact.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
